problems.problem: The batch carries the sentence whose revision was refuted on form, and that refutation’s point still applies to it. In ‘beneath the tree where his old rags hung whenever discontent came’, the clause ‘whenever discontent came’ attaches to ‘hung’, so the sentence says the rags hung only when discontent came. In Burlingame XXV.10, ‘whenever he became discontented’ governs his going to the tree and admonishing himself. The src also still lacks the Norman pages (pp. 115 to 116) that the verifier opened, although every other Burlingame src in the batch gives them.
problems.fix: Use the refuter’s reorder, which passes entry-check (scratch/crit-fix25.json): “Late in the chapter on the mendicant, the verse addresses him directly; the Theravāda commentary, Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā XXV.10, reads it as spoken for a former ploughman who, whenever discontent came, admonished himself beneath the tree where his old rags hung, and so became an arahat.” Use src “The Theravāda commentary, Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā XXV.10 (on verses 379 to 380), trans. Burlingame, Buddhist Legends, vol. 3 (1921), Norman pp. 115 to 116” (152 characters).

problems.problem: Prose and exactness. The reading gives the commentary’s reason in terms of ‘the stream-enterer’, but it never says that the commentary takes the verse’s ‘first step in holiness’ as stream-entry (Sotāpattiphalaṃ varanti … sotāpattiphalameva varaṃ uttamanti attho). A reader who does not know the term is left with no link between the key verse and the reason given. ‘A world-ruler’ also narrows the commentary’s ‘one who has exercised rule over so great a domain’, which covers earth, heaven and all worlds.
problems.fix: Give the identification, then the reason, in the commentary’s terms. This passes entry-check (scratch/crit-fix13.json): “The chapter on the world ends by setting one attainment above every kingdom and heaven; the Theravāda commentary, on verse 178, takes it as stream-entry, for a ruler of so much is not freed from hell, while the stream-enterer has shut the doors to woe.”
